Summarized from university agriculture guides. Variety-specific seed packet directions take priority.
Check the plant type and seed count.
Use a sterile, soilless, fine-textured and well-drained seed-starting mix; do not use garden soil.
Start with a 72–128-cell tray and sow 1 seed per cell. Check the variety’s packet directions.
Use a sterile, soilless, fine-textured and well-drained seed-starting mix; do not use garden soil.
A 72-cell tray is suitable; sow 1 seed per cell. Choose larger cells if seedlings will be held longer.
Use a sterile, soilless, airy and free-draining seed-starting mix; do not leave it waterlogged.
A 72-cell tray is suitable; sow 1 seed per cell. Move slow-growing seedlings before they become root-bound.
Use a sterile, airy and fast-draining seed-starting mix; do not leave the root zone saturated.
Use a large 50-cell tray or individual pots; sow 1 seed per cell and keep the root ball intact.
Use a sterile, soilless, fine-textured and well-drained seed-starting mix; keep it warm and evenly moist.
A 72-cell tray is suitable; sow 1 seed per cell. Pot up if the growing period will be long.
Prepare warm, loose and well-drained garden soil; do not allow water to stand.
No tray is needed; direct sowing beans in their final location reduces root damage.
Use deep, loose, stone-free and well-drained sandy loam; compacted soil can deform roots.
Do not use a tray; direct sow carrots in their final location because the taproot develops early.
Use a warm, loose and well-drained medium; choose sterile seed-starting mix when using trays.
Direct sowing is possible; for transplants use deep 50-cell trays, sow 1 seed per cell and transplant young.
Use a sterile, airy and well-drained seed-starting mix; avoid waterlogged conditions.
Use a large 50-cell tray or individual pots; sow 1 seed per cell and keep the root ball intact.
Use a fine-textured, sterile mix that retains moisture while draining well.
A 128-cell tray is suitable; sow 1–2 seeds per cell and thin to 1 seedling after emergence.
Use a fine-textured, sterile and well-drained seed-starting mix; keep the surface evenly moist.
A 128–200-cell tray is suitable; sow 1–2 seeds per cell and do not let roots become crowded.
Use loose, light and well-drained soil that can be hilled as tubers develop.
No tray is needed; plant certified seed tubers or pieces carrying at least 1–2 eyes directly in soil.
Prepare warm, loose and well-drained garden soil.
No tray is needed; direct sowing in the final location is preferred because corn transplants poorly.
Prepare cool, loose and well-drained garden soil; avoid wet, airless conditions.
No tray is needed; direct sowing peas in their final location avoids disturbing the roots.
Use well-drained loam or sandy loam and keep the crown level with the soil surface when planting.
A tray is usually unnecessary; prefer healthy bare-root plants or plugs. Follow packet directions if growing from seed.
Use a sterile, airy and well-drained seed-starting mix; keep it warm without overwatering.
Use a large 50-cell tray or individual pots; sow 1 hybrid or 1–2 open-pollinated seeds and avoid root disturbance.
Use a sterile, airy and well-drained seed-starting mix; keep it warm and evenly moist.
Use a large 50-cell tray or individual pots; sow 1 seed per cell and transplant with the root ball intact.
Extra fertilizer may be unnecessary when the mix already contains nutrients. Do not fertilize dry, wilted, waterlogged or diseased seedlings, and never exceed the product label.
Do not fertilize; provide only clean water and suitable moisture.
A fully soluble, balanced NPK fertilizer with trace elements labeled for seedlings.
A fully soluble, balanced NPK plus trace-element seedling fertilizer at a controlled moderate concentration.
A fully soluble, balanced NPK plus trace-element seedling fertilizer at low concentration.
A balanced, soluble complete fertilizer with moderate nitrogen at low concentration.
A balanced soluble seedling fertilizer supplying nitrogen and phosphorus for early root growth.
No routine nitrogen fertilizer; supply phosphorus or potassium only when testing shows a deficiency.
Low-nitrogen nutrition with phosphorus and potassium based on soil testing.
A soil-test-based complete N-P-K program; consider additional nitrogen after emergence during hilling.
Soil-test-based starter phosphorus and planned nitrogen; fertilizer must not touch the seed.
Phosphorus, potassium and moderate nitrogen based on soil and leaf testing.
A fully soluble, balanced NPK plus trace-element fertilizer at low to moderate concentration.
A balanced, soluble NPK plus trace-element fertilizer labeled for seedlings, at low concentration.
Do not add a new or stronger feed; do not increase the existing low-concentration program.
A soil-test-based starter with moderate nitrogen and phosphorus-potassium only when needed.
A low-nitrogen starter based on soil testing; avoid excess salts and nitrogen.
A balanced starter or preplant fertilizer based on soil testing; avoid excess nitrogen.
Test-based phosphorus-potassium and moderate nitrogen; split nitrogen after roots establish.
No routine nitrogen; use the appropriate Rhizobium inoculant and phosphorus-potassium only when tests indicate need.
Low-nitrogen, test-based phosphorus-potassium nutrition; avoid excess nitrogen.
A soil-test-based complete N-P-K program; split later nitrogen between emergence and hilling.
Soil-test-based starter phosphorus and a seasonal nitrogen plan; band fertilizer away from seed.
Preplant phosphorus-potassium and part of the total nitrogen based on soil testing.
A balanced starter based on soil testing; avoid excess nitrogen.
A balanced starter fertilizer selected from soil-test results.
Keep fertilizer away from seed. Do not add more fertilizer to a seed-starting mix that already contains nutrients.
Do not use liquid fertilizer until cotyledons are fully open and the first true leaf begins to appear.
If the first true leaf is opening and the mix has no fertilizer, start on moist mix at one-quarter label strength; use up to half strength only when the label permits seedling use.
Apply to moist mix about weekly; do not increase if growth is balanced and medium green. Follow the seedling directions on every product.
Do not starve seedlings by suddenly stopping nutrition. Harden over 5–7 days using light, air movement and controlled watering.
At planting, use starter solution on a moist root ball only when supported by testing and the label; keep it off stems and leaves.
Do not use transplant starter; follow soil-test results and the crop-specific note in the final growing location.
Tomato transplants can use slightly stronger feeding than cucurbits, but excess nitrogen causes soft, overly leafy growth.
Use regular but low-salt nutrition for pepper; excess nitrogen and concentration can produce weak transplants.
Cucumber and other cucurbits need lower fertilizer concentration than tomato and pepper; protect sensitive roots from burn.
Control nitrogen for eggplant; excess nitrogen can promote foliage and delay flowering.
A bean-specific Rhizobium inoculant may help at sowing; use soil testing instead of routine nitrogen.
Excess nitrogen favors tops over roots and may contribute to misshapen roots.
Use balanced, moderate nutrition for okra; avoid excessive nitrogen and unnecessary soft vegetative growth.
Use low-concentration complete fertilizer for squash seedlings and prevent salt accumulation in the root ball.
Lettuce is shallow-rooted and needs measured nitrogen; excess can cause soft growth and increase tipburn risk.
Onions benefit from early phosphorus and steady nitrogen; heavy or late nitrogen harms maturity and storage quality.
Potatoes have relatively high nutrient demand; plan by testing and split later nitrogen with post-emergence hilling.
Corn needs nitrogen; use starter phosphorus only when needed and never place fertilizer against seed.
Use a pea-specific Rhizobium inoculant; supplemental nitrogen is usually unnecessary when nodulation is healthy.
Set phosphorus, potassium and nitrogen from testing; excess nitrogen promotes foliage and runners over fruit.
Use low-concentration complete fertilizer for watermelon transplants; excess may burn roots and cause overgrowth.
Use low-concentration complete fertilizer for melon transplants and prevent salt buildup in the root ball.
Cole-crop transplants respond to complete feed; avoid sustained high nitrogen and set field rates by soil testing.
After the first true leaf, use low-concentration balanced fertilizer for parsley and avoid high salts.
For this legume, crop-specific Rhizobium inoculation and soil testing matter more than routine nitrogen fertilizer.
Use moderate nitrogen for this leafy crop and avoid promoting rapid, soft growth.
Early phosphorus and moderate nitrogen may help this allium; soil testing should determine exact amounts.
For a user-added crop, determine exact fertilizer ratios from soil or medium testing and the variety’s production label.
